title: Viagra May Slow the Spread of Cancer
gist: A Weizmann Institute-led study in Cancer Research reports that sildenafil’s PDE5 blockade raises cGMP, which binds a cholesterol-transport protein cancer cells rely on to build membranes for metastasis — identifying an off-target anti-metastatic mechanism in mouse and human cancer cells. The subhead promises a statin angle that the truncated text never develops.

insights.claim: Sildenafil was developed by Pfizer as a treatment for chest pain and high blood pressure, and only became Viagra after male test subjects reported unexpected side effects — a reminder the compound’s commercial identity was always a repurposing.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A cheap, off-patent, extensively safety-characterized molecule is the ideal substrate for a new oncology indication.
insights.locator: Viagra was something of an accident

insights.claim: A study in Cancer Research proposes sildenafil as a means of preventing the metastasis of cancer cells, a second repurposing of the same molecule.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Watch for follow-on trials; a generic PDE5 inhibitor with anti-metastatic effect would be low-cost and fast to test.
insights.locator: Now sildenafil might have another use

themes.theme: cGMP, cholesterol transport, and membrane supply

insights.claim: Sildenafil works by blocking phosphodiesterase type 5, which normally degrades cyclic GMP, so inhibiting PDE5 lets cGMP accumulate and relaxes blood vessel walls.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The known mechanism is the entry point — the anti-cancer effect rides on the same cGMP accumulation, not a new target.
insights.locator: Sildenafil works by blocking the activity of phosphodiesterase type 5

insights.claim: Elevated cGMP binds a protein that transports cholesterol inside cells, the raw material used to build cell membranes — an unrecognized second job for a well-studied second messenger.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Links a cardiovascular signaling pathway to lipid supply, a route that also connects to cholesterol-lowering drugs.
insights.quote: They discovered cGMP has a side hustle, just like sildenafil.
insights.locator: Researchers led by a team from the Weizmann Institute

insights.claim: Cancer cells that are striking out to colonize other parts of the body depend on newly built membranes and are particularly vulnerable to the supply disruption caused by elevated cGMP activity.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Predicts the effect is specific to metastasis rather than primary tumor growth — the endpoint any trial should measure.
insights.locator: These membranes come in handy for cancer cells

insights.claim: The findings come from sildenafil treatment of both mouse and human cancer cells cultured from a variety of cancers, led by a team from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Preclinical cell-culture stage only — no in-human evidence, so treat the metastasis claim as hypothesis-generating.
insights.locator: treated mouse and human cancer cells
